title: Load-Bearing People
author: Mike Fisher
summary: Fisher takes the 2016 left-pad incident, in which a developer's protest removal of eleven lines of JavaScript broke builds at Facebook, Netflix, Spotify, PayPal and Airbnb, and uses it to make key person risk legible to leaders outside engineering. His claim is that every function has a left-pad: the analyst who knows how the quarterly close actually runs rather than how it is documented, the account executive holding the relationships with the three largest customers, the person a critical vendor will pick up the phone for. He then explains why these people stay invisible, arguing that heroics get rewarded while the runbook that prevents the midnight call gets nothing, that redundancy reads as trimmable slack on a spreadsheet, and that indispensability feels good to the person carrying it. The XZ Utils backdoor of 2024 supplies the darker case, where an exhausted volunteer maintainer was cultivated for two years by an attacker and the save came down to one engineer curious about half a second of latency. The remedies are a bus-factor audit, a vacation test read as fragility rather than dedication, recognition redirected to fireproofers, and redundancy treated as a design principle.
points: The left-pad outage is used to show that dependency chains nobody had traced can concentrate enormous weight on one unpaid person.
Fisher insists the pattern is not an engineering curiosity, naming the equivalent load-bearing person in finance, sales, operations, legal and HR.
He argues that strong teams generate more of these people, because hard work keeps getting routed to whoever handles it best.
Three incentives keep the risk hidden: heroics get applauded, redundancy looks like waste, and being indispensable feels good.
The vacation test is offered as the cheapest available diagnostic, with degradation during a two week absence read as fragility rather than devotion.
quotes: Koçulu objected and, in protest, unpublished all 273 packages he maintained. Among them was a tiny package called left-pad . It was eleven lines of code that added spaces to the front of a text string so it lined up.

Popular tools required it, other tools required those tools, and eleven lines of string padding held up a large share of the JavaScript ecosystem. No one had traced the chain, because nothing had ever forced anyone to.

A bus-factor of one means one person understands billing reconciliation, or holds the only working knowledge of the legacy service, or knows how a Friday release gets deployed. That person is your left-pad.

Wherever hard won, undocumented knowledge sits in one head, you have a load-bearing human. The stronger your team, the more of them you have, because you keep routing the hard work to whoever handles it best.

The person who swoops in at midnight to fix the thing only they understand gets praised and promoted. The colleague who spent that same week writing the runbook that would have prevented the midnight call gets nothing, because you cannot celebrate an outage that never happened.
Cross training a second person on one critical job costs real time this quarter to protect against a loss that may never arrive. On a spreadsheet it reads as slack, and slack gets trimmed.

Two weeks off the grid is the cheapest diagnostic you own. If the operation degrades while someone is on a beach, you found a single point of failure at the best possible price, since the person is still reachable if it gets bad enough.
Treat a bus-factor of one the way you treat a production server with no backup, as a defect with an owner and a due date.
